props.title: Odds Against Tomorrow
props.initialSlug: Racial tensions explode in a desperate heist plot

sections.content: **Odds Against Tomorrow** (1959) stands as one of the last and most potent film noirs, injecting searing racial commentary into its heist framework. Robert Wise directs Harry Belafonte and Robert Ryan in a taut thriller where racial tensions explode during a bank robbery scheme. The film builds on earlier noir examinations of prejudice like **Crossfire** (1947) and **No Way Out** (1950), but pushes further by making racism the central powder keg that dooms its characters. Wise's stark black-and-white cinematography and jazz score (featuring Modern Jazz Quartet) create a pressure cooker atmosphere.

sections.content: The film represents a bridge between classic noir and the social consciousness of 1960s cinema. Its influence can be traced through later heist films dealing with racial dynamics like In the Heat of the Night (1967) and **Dead Presidents** (1995). Wise's direction emphasizes psychological tension through tight close-ups and dramatic shadows, while the screenplay by Abraham Polonsky (blacklisted at the time) layers in sharp social commentary without sacrificing the genre's punchy dialogue and fatalistic mood.

Harry Belafonte's production company HarBel helped bring this progressive noir to screen, making it one of the first major Hollywood films to directly confront racial prejudice through a crime story lens. The film's ending, where prejudice literally destroys both men, was shocking for 1959 audiences. It influenced later neo-noirs like **Devil in a Blue Dress** (1995) and **Deep Cover** (1992) that explored similar themes of race and crime. SUBHEAD: Jazz Noir and Visual Style

movies.title: In the Heat of the Night
movies.slug: Sidney Poitier and Rod Steiger star in this Oscar-winning crime drama about a Black detective working a murder case in the racist South

sections.content: The film's groundbreaking jazz score by John Lewis of the Modern Jazz Quartet helped establish a new sonic template for noir, moving beyond traditional orchestral scores. This approach influenced later crime films like **Cotton Comes to Harlem** (1970) and **Shaft** (1971). Wise's documentary-style location shooting in New York and Hudson, NY creates a gritty realism that would become standard in 1970s crime films like **The French Connection** (1971) and **Serpico** (1973).
